                    ### Question
                    A 40-year-old male visits a urologist and reports that for the past 2 weeks, his penis has been gradually curving to the right with associated pain during intercourse. He is able to have a normal erection and he does not recollect of any trauma to his penis. Although he is married, he admits to having unprotected sexual relationship with several females in the past year. His vitals are normal and physical examination in unremarkable except for a lesionless curved penis. It is painless to touch. Test results for sexually transmitted disease is pending. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Fibrosis of corpus cavernosa
opb. Congenital hypospadias
opc. Syphilitic chancre
opd. Fibrosis of tunica albuginea
ope. Hypertrophy of corpus cavernosa

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely cause of the patient's symptoms, including gradual curvature of the penis and pain during intercourse without recollection of trauma, is Peyronie's disease. This condition is characterized by fibrosis of the tunica albuginea, which aligns with the observed symptoms and the absence of lesions or other abnormalities on physical examination. The evidence path linking fibrosis to Peyronie's disease supports this diagnosis. Other options such as syphilitic chancre and hypertrophy of corpus cavernosa are less likely due to the absence of typical clinical findings and the patient's history not strongly supporting these conditions. Congenital hypospadias is also unlikely given the late onset of symptoms. Therefore, the diagnosis of Peyronie's disease, supported by the fibrosis of tunica albuginea, is the most consistent with the patient's presentation and available medical consensus.
